# Five functions, one organization: reading the viable system model against an AI-run firm

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that if the reports from an AI system's agents all say green, the organization is healthy. This paper argues otherwise: beer's model keeps a channel that checks operations directly instead of through their own reports. In software that means proving each deploy live against its commit, not reading the agent's account of it.

Stafford Beer applied Ashby's cybernetics to organizations in his viable system model: operations, coordination, control, intelligence and policy, each recursive. We ask whether an AI-run system has an owner for each function and an independent way to check that operations match the reports about them.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 3 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

A viable organization has operational units that do the work, coordination among them, control of their resources, an intelligence function that watches the outside and the future, and a policy function that settles identity. Each operational unit can itself be a viable system. A separate audit channel checks operations directly, rather than through the reports operations make about themselves. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, green reports mean a healthy organization, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A unit that is not itself viable. Each operational unit of the organization must be able to run and correct itself: its own code, clock, probe and settler. A unit that depends on a central manager for every correction is not an operational unit but an instruction. [1]
2. Operations judged by their own reports. An audit channel reads reality directly. A deploy is counted only when the live Worker's version matches the commit, read through a different path from the deploy itself. [1]
3. Intelligence with no memory of what it learned. The intelligence function must turn what it learns about the environment into something the rest of the organization can use. The system keeps a graph of its own data, and every system carries one. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A unit that is not itself viable: every manager owns loops and the code that settles what it files (MANAGERS-1, `doctrine/managers.json`); the managers check (MANAGERS-1, `foundation/managers.py`)
2. Operations judged by their own reports: each deploy row records whether the live version matched the commit (DEPLOY-VERIFIED-1, `ops/deploys.jsonl`); progress counts only merged behaviour change (PROGRESS-1, `seed/worker/src/progress.js`)
3. Intelligence with no memory of what it learned: every system declares a knowledge graph, built or pending (DATAGRAPH-1, `doctrine/knowledge-graph.json`); the graph is built and read each pass (DATAGRAPH-1, `seed/worker/src/datagraph.js`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A unit that is not itself viable. Put in place: every manager owns loops and the code that settles what it files. Check it with one number, share of manager roles in doctrine/managers.json that name code, a clock, a closing probe and the code that settles what they file, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. Operations judged by their own reports. Put in place: each deploy row records whether the live version matched the commit. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
3. Intelligence with no memory of what it learned. Put in place: every system declares a knowledge graph, built or pending. Check it with one number, share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 3 of 3 of these checks pass today. Share of manager roles in doctrine/managers.json that name code, a clock, a closing probe and the code that settles what they file reads 1.0 (n = 18; source: doctrine/managers.json). Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit reads 0.999 (n = 980; source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window)). Share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending reads 1.0 (n = 5; source: doctrine/knowledge-graph.json (declared)). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Reading. The source was not machine-read for this paper: its argument is stated in our own words from the publication's well-known content, with no quotation, and a reader should check the claim against the source linked above.
- Mapping. Mapping an AI system's managers onto Beer's five systems is our interpretation; this paper measures that each manager is closed (owns code, clock, probe, settler) and that deploys are proven live by an independent read, not that the mapping is the only valid one.
- Scope. Beer's model is also a claim about people in organizations; nothing here is a claim about people.
- Scale. One organization: 500 closed pull requests (378 merged) over 6.96 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 89% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the self-sustaining regime with 33 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Book, version 1972; its findings may change in later versions.
